faq.q: Why is leaping easier than swimming at speed?
faq.a: At high speed the drag of water is huge, especially near the surface where the dolphin makes waves. In the air there is far less drag, so a leap carries the dolphin forward cheaply before it dives back in.

faq.q: How do dolphins breathe while swimming?
faq.a: Dolphins breathe through a blowhole on top of the head, which opens only at the surface. Leaping or surfacing lets them breathe out and in within a fraction of a second, then a muscular flap seals it again.

faq.q: How do dolphins swim so fast?
faq.a: Dolphins beat their tail flukes up and down using strong back muscles, and their smooth, torpedo-shaped body makes little drag. Bottlenose dolphins can burst to about 30 kilometres per hour.

Why does a dolphin's tail move up and down?

faq.q: Why does a dolphin's tail move up and down, not side to side?
faq.a: Dolphins evolved from land mammals whose spines bend up and down when they run. When their ancestors returned to the sea they kept that up-and-down bend, unlike fish, whose bodies bend side to side.
asks: Why do dolphin tails flap vertically?

faq.a: Some leaps look playful, and dolphins do play, ride waves and spin. Leaps and splashes may also signal to other dolphins or help herd fish, so a jump can have more than one reason.
asks: Why do dolphins spin in the air?

facts: Water is roughly 800 times denser than air at sea level.
Dolphin tail flukes contain no bones; they are stiffened by tough fibrous tissue.
